questions.q: What is a Service Level Indicator (SLI)?
options: The server's CPU and memory utilization graphed over time
A single, measured, user-facing metric — such as availability or latency — usually expressed as a ratio or percentage
The dollar penalty written into a customer contract
A dashboard showing every metric a team could possibly track
questions.explain: An SLI is a concrete measured metric that reflects user experience, like the fraction of requests that succeeded or completed under a latency threshold — not an internal health signal like CPU.

questions.q: An SLO of "99.9% availability over a rolling 30 days" differs from the same percentage measured over a single day mainly because:
options: The two windows are mathematically identical and the difference is cosmetic
A daily window always allows more downtime than a 30-day window
A short, sharp outage barely dents a 30-day budget but can blow an entire daily budget on its own
SLOs can only be measured in dollars, never in time windows
questions.explain: The time window changes how much a single outage matters: a brief outage that consumes a whole day's budget is a small fraction of a 30-day budget, so the window is as important as the percentage itself.

questions.q: How is an error budget calculated from an SLO?
options: It is set independently by finance and has no formula
Error budget equals 100% minus the SLO target, expressed over the SLO's time window
It equals the number of support tickets filed that month
It equals the SLA penalty amount divided by monthly revenue
questions.explain: If the SLO target is 99.9%, the error budget is the remaining 0.1% of the time window — roughly 43 minutes over a rolling 30 days.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between an SLO and an SLA, as this lesson describes them?
options: An SLO is the external contractual promise and an SLA is the internal engineering target — the reverse of the common naming
They are the same thing; SLA is just an older name for SLO
SLAs only apply to latency, while SLOs only apply to availability
An SLO is the internal engineering target; an SLA is the external, usually looser, contractual promise to customers with financial penalties attached
questions.explain: The SLO is the internal target engineering holds itself to. The SLA is the external, contractual commitment to customers, deliberately set looser so there's margin to catch a problem before it breaches a paying customer's agreement.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that a 100% reliability target is actually counterproductive?
options: Because a service with zero error budget has zero room to take any risk, including deploying new code, since every deploy carries some nonzero chance of a brief disruption
Because 100% reliability is illegal under most SLAs
Because customers always prefer lower reliability to save money
Because monitoring tools cannot measure values above 99%
questions.explain: An error budget isn't just a tolerance for failure — it's what gives a team room to ship at all. At 100%, there is no room left to take the small risk every deploy carries, so shipping effectively stops.
